why.correct: Eustress is stress felt as a motivating challenge; distress is stress felt as harmful.
options: Distress is harmful, overwhelming stress; Ines feels energized and challenged.
Right: positive stress that motivates and feels like a challenge.
Daily hassles are small, everyday annoyances, not a major positive life change.
Exhaustion follows long, unrelenting stress; she is just starting and energized.

why.correct: Daily hassles are minor everyday stressors; their buildup predicts health problems.
options: Catastrophes are large-scale disasters, such as earthquakes or wars.
These annoyances are not motivating challenges.
Adverse childhood experiences are serious early events such as abuse or neglect.
Right: small, everyday irritations that can add up and affect health.

why.correct: Fight-flight-freeze is the fast, automatic response to threat driven by sympathetic arousal.
options: Right: under sudden threat, the body may freeze as well as fight or flee.
Tend-and-befriend means caring for others and seeking support, not going still.
Problem-focused coping is a planned effort to change the stressor, not an automatic reaction.
The resistance stage comes after the first alarm, during long-term stress.

why.correct: Tend-and-befriend: under stress, people protect those close to them and seek social support; it was first described in women and is linked to oxytocin.
options: They are not fighting, fleeing or freezing; they are caring for others.
The alarm reaction is the body's first sympathetic arousal, not the social behavior described.
Right: protecting offspring (tend) and seeking support from others (befriend).
They are building support, not refusing to accept what happened.

why.correct: Problem-focused coping tackles the stressor itself.
options: Emotion-focused coping manages the feelings rather than changing the stressor.
Right: she takes direct action on the cause of her stress.
Displacement is a defense mechanism that moves feelings to a safer target.
Exhaustion is a stage of long-term stress, not a coping strategy.

why.correct: Emotion-focused coping regulates feelings; it suits stressors we cannot control.
options: Right: when a stressor cannot be changed, managing the emotional response is often the better fit.
There is no problem he can act on to change the loss.
That is an automatic response to sudden threat, not a chosen coping strategy.
Sensation seeking is a trait of seeking intense experiences.

why.correct: Flexible coping: problem-focused for what is controllable, emotion-focused for what is not.
options: Problem-focused coping often works well when a person has some control.
Avoidance tends to predict worse outcomes over time.
Trying to fix what cannot be changed adds frustration.
Right: matching the strategy to how controllable the stressor is works best.

why.correct: Correlation is not causation: name possible third variables.
options: The study is correlational, and many people with these experiences stay healthy.
Right: the data are correlational, so third variables such as income or smoking could play a role.
This reverses the timing; still, memory bias is worth noting.
The study found higher rates in the group with more adverse experiences.

why.correct: Health psychology studies how psychological and social factors affect physical health.
options: I/O psychology studies behavior in the workplace.
Developmental psychology studies change across the lifespan.
Right: health psychology links mind, behavior and physical health.
Evolutionary psychology studies how natural selection shaped behavior.

why.correct: In resistance the body's defenses stay raised while the stressor continues.
options: The alarm reaction is the brief dip at the start, around week 1.
Right: the index stays well above normal as the body copes with the continuing stressor.
Exhaustion is when the index falls below normal, around weeks 10 to 12.
The placement is still going on in weeks 3 to 7.

why.correct: Exhaustion: reserves run down after prolonged stress, and vulnerability to illness rises.
options: Weeks 10 to 12 are at the end of the placement, not the start.
Long, demanding stress here is distress, and eustress is no guarantee of health.
The graph shows the index falling below normal at the end.
Right: the index fell below 100, matching the exhaustion stage and more illness.

why.correct: <math class="psy-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>118</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>120</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>119</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>120</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>117</mn></mrow><mn>5</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{118 + 120 + 119 + 120 + 117}{5}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="psy-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mn>594</mn><mn>5</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{594}{5}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="psy-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>118.8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 118.8</annotation></semantics></math>.
Following one group over time without a comparison group cannot rule out other causes.
options: Right: without a control group, a third variable that changed over time could explain the pattern.
Saliva can be used for some immune measures; the issue is the design.
Thirty is a small sample, and size is not the main problem.
Line graphs are the standard way to show change over time.

why.correct: Alarm: a brief drop at the shock of the stressor, then the sympathetic system mobilizes the body.
options: That describes exhaustion, at the end of the curve.
The figure shows a body response, not a coping choice.
Right: the alarm stage starts with shock, then sympathetic arousal.
The figure shows a stressor that continues.

why.correct: Exhaustion follows long, unrelenting stress.
options: Alarm is the start of a stressor, not two years in.
In resistance the body is still coping; frequent illness points to the next stage.
His frequent illness suggests resistance has fallen below normal.
Right: after prolonged stress, reserves run down and illness becomes more likely.

why.correct: The stages describe a general pattern; appraisal, coping and support change it for individuals.
options: Animal findings often generalize in part; human research has supported the broad pattern.
Right: the stages describe the body's response, and appraisal and coping shape how strongly it happens.
Short-term stress and eustress can be helpful.
People differ a great deal in how quickly stress affects them, so the speed is not fixed.

why.correct: Measuring a relationship without manipulating anything is correlational.
options: The researchers did not manipulate hassles or assign people to conditions.
A case study examines one person in depth; this one followed 150 people.
Right: it measured how two variables, hassles and symptom days, were related.
Participants reported their own hassles; no one observed them.

why.correct: Read direction and strength from r; a correlation is not a cause.
options: Right: a positive r below about .4 is weak to moderate.
A positive r means the two rose together.
A correlation does not show cause or a percentage of cases.
An r of 0.35 shows some relationship.

why.correct: Always name a possible third variable for a correlation.
options: A larger sample makes a link more trustworthy, not less.
Rating hassles cannot cause colds.
No one was assigned to have hassles.
Right: a third variable, such as poor sleep, could explain both.

why.correct: Give the measure the study used: a 0 to 10 rating each evening, averaged over eight weeks.
The same stressor can produce distress or eustress depending on appraisal.
options: Right: stress depends on how we appraise a stressor and our ability to handle it.
It is the same exam for both students.
Nothing suggests either has had a long-lasting stressor.
Nothing suggests a difference in their nervous systems; the difference is in how they see the exam.

why.correct: Positive psychology studies human flourishing scientifically.
options: Health psychology studies how stress and behavior affect physical health and illness.
The psychodynamic approach studies unconscious conflicts, not flourishing.
Right: the scientific study of well-being, strengths and what helps people and communities thrive.
I/O psychology studies workplaces, but this team studies flourishing in all areas of life.

why.correct: Subjective well-being is self-reported happiness and life satisfaction.
options: Right: a person's own judgment of life satisfaction plus the balance of positive and negative feelings.
Resilience is bouncing back from adversity; nothing here is about recovering from a hardship.
Self-efficacy is belief in succeeding at a task, not satisfaction with life.
Eustress is positive stress, not a rating of life satisfaction.

why.correct: Resilience: recovering and adapting well after adversity, which is common.
options: Growth would mean positive change beyond her earlier level, such as new priorities; she returned to her earlier functioning.
Right: adapting well and bouncing back after adversity.
Learned helplessness is giving up after repeated uncontrollable events; she recovered.
Denial would be refusing to accept the loss; she was shaken and then adapted.

why.correct: Posttraumatic growth: positive change, such as new priorities or closer relationships, after struggling with trauma.
options: Resilience is returning to the earlier level; Dev describes positive change beyond it.
Reaction formation is a defense mechanism showing the opposite of a hidden feeling.
Eustress is positive stress at the time; Dev describes lasting change after a trauma.
Right: positive psychological change after struggling with a highly challenging event.

why.correct: Gratitude practices ask people to notice and appreciate what is good.
options: Right: noticing and appreciating good things in life.
Self-actualization is a humanistic idea about growing toward potential, not a daily writing practice.
Resilience is recovering from adversity; the exercise targets appreciation of good events.
Display rules are cultural norms for showing emotion.

why.correct: Signature strengths are a person's most characteristic strengths; using them is linked to well-being.
options: The Big Five are broad trait dimensions, not the strengths a person uses most and values most.
Defense mechanisms protect against anxiety, not strengths that feel authentic.
Right: the character strengths a person shows most and that feel most central to who they are.
The six virtues are the broad groups; his personal top strengths are his signature strengths.

why.correct: Report findings at their real size: positive psychology exercises show small average effects.
options: The effects were small, and not every study finds them lasting.
Right: positive psychology interventions tend to show small average effects.
The scenario does not show that; effects vary across people.
Happiness gains after an exercise say nothing about heredity.

why.correct: Bravery is a courage strength.
options: Wisdom covers strengths of knowledge such as curiosity and perspective.
Right: bravery, acting on what is right despite risk, is a strength of courage.
Temperance covers self-control strengths such as prudence and forgiveness.
Transcendence covers strengths that connect us to something larger, such as gratitude and hope.

why.correct: Fairness, leadership and teamwork are justice strengths.
options: Humanity covers close, one-on-one strengths such as love and kindness.
Wisdom covers strengths such as curiosity and perspective.
Transcendence covers strengths such as gratitude, hope and humor.
Right: fairness and leadership are strengths of justice, which support healthy group life.

why.correct: Forgiveness and self-regulation belong to temperance.
options: Right: forgiveness and self-regulation are temperance strengths that protect against excess.
Courage covers bravery and perseverance in the face of difficulty.
Justice covers strengths of group life, such as fairness and teamwork.
Wisdom covers strengths of knowledge and judgment such as curiosity.

why.correct: <math class="psy-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>5.3</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>4.8</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0.5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5.3 - 4.8 = 0.5</annotation></semantics></math> points.
Significance says a difference is unlikely to be chance; effect size says how big it is.
options: A small effect size means the difference was modest, and it is an average, not true of each student.
Statistically significant means the difference is unlikely to be due to chance alone.
Right: significance and size are different questions.
Random assignment makes this an experiment.

why.correct: A control group lets researchers separate the effect of the treatment from other changes.
options: Adding a control group keeps it an experiment.
Right: the control group shows what changes without gratitude, so the gap can be credited to gratitude.
A control group does not change the true effect; it makes the comparison fair.
Confidentiality is about data privacy, not about having a control group.

why.correct: Resilience is common, a key finding in research on adversity; the support finding is a correlation.
options: Right: 62% showed low distress throughout, more than the other two groups combined.
Only 15% were in the chronic group.
Support was measured, not manipulated, so this correlational result cannot show cause.
Resilience was the most common pattern here.

why.correct: Measuring the same people repeatedly over time is longitudinal.
options: A cross-sectional design compares different people at one time; here the same people were measured three times.
A case study examines one or a few people in depth; this study followed 480.
Right: the same participants were measured at 3, 12 and 24 months.
Nothing was manipulated, and no one was randomly assigned.

why.correct: <math class="psy-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>100</mn><mo>%</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>62</mn><mo>%</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>38</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">100\% - 62\% = 38\%</annotation></semantics></math> (or <math class="psy-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>23</mn><mo>%</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">+</mo><mn>15</mn><mo>%</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>38</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">23\% + 15\% = 38\%</annotation></semantics></math>).
Generalize from participant characteristics: age, place and type of event.
options: Sample size is not the main issue; who the participants were is.
The scale range does not limit generalizing to another group.
Confidentiality is an ethical safeguard, not a limit on generalizing.
Right: age, culture and the kind of disaster all differ from the new population.

why.correct: An operational definition names the measure and the rule: low distress scores at all three times.
Positive psychology makes careful claims: modest links, mostly correlational, not cures.
options: Positive psychology has not shown that optimism cures disease.
Subjective well-being is a self-report measure, not a treatment.
Right: research shows modest associations, mostly correlational, and blaming patients for not being positive enough is unfair.
Happiness can be studied scientifically; the problem is the overstated claim.

why.correct: Dysfunction means the pattern interferes with work, school, relationships or self-care; her missed classes and lost job are exactly that.
options: Deviation is about how unusual a pattern is in its culture. Missed classes and a lost job show interference with life, not unusualness.
Distress is the inner pain she feels. The missed classes and lost job are about what she can no longer do.
A diathesis is a vulnerability in the diathesis-stress model, a possible cause, not part of the definition.
Right: missing classes and losing a job are signs that the pattern interferes with daily functioning.

why.correct: A pattern counts as a disorder when it is unusual and also causes distress or gets in the way of life. Being different is not a disorder.
options: His habits are unusual, so deviation is present. What is missing is distress and dysfunction.
Living alone does not prevent a diagnosis. What matters is whether the pattern causes distress or dysfunction.
Right: deviation alone is not enough. A disorder also involves distress or dysfunction, and Theo shows neither.
Diathesis is a possible cause, not part of the definition, and nothing in the scenario tells us about it.

why.correct: The sociocultural perspective reminds clinicians that what counts as unusual depends on the culture. A behavior expected in mourning is not deviant in that setting.
options: Distress is one part of the definition, but the error here is about cultural norms, not distress.
Right: speaking to the dead is expected in that community, so it is not deviant there. Judging it by the clinician's home norms is the mistake.
Grief is a normal response to loss, and the model does not say grief alone causes a disorder.
The opposite is true: whether a behavior is unusual depends on its cultural context.

why.correct: The ICD comes from the World Health Organization and covers all health conditions; the DSM-5-TR comes from the American Psychiatric Association.
options: Right: the ICD is the World Health Organization's system, used worldwide for physical and psychological conditions.
The DSM-5-TR is published by the American Psychiatric Association, not the World Health Organization.
The biopsychosocial model explains causes. It is not a system of diagnostic codes.
The eclectic approach means drawing on several perspectives. It is not a classification system.

why.correct: The behavioral perspective explains a disorder by learning: the bite paired dogs with pain, and the relief of avoiding dogs reinforces the avoidance.
options: A psychodynamic explanation would point to unconscious conflicts, not to learning from a bite.
A humanistic explanation would focus on self-concept and growth, not on conditioning.
An evolutionary explanation would say fears of dangerous animals helped ancestors survive. The psychologist talks about Luis's own learning.
Right: the explanation uses learning, classical conditioning for the fear and negative reinforcement for the avoidance.

why.correct: The cognitive perspective explains disorders through patterns of thinking, such as overgeneralizing one failure into a belief about oneself.
options: A biological explanation would point to genes, brain structures or neurotransmitters, not her interpretation of a grade.
A sociocultural explanation would look at her culture, family or social conditions, not her own thought pattern.
Right: the cognitive perspective looks at thoughts and interpretations, such as turning one low grade into proof of failure.
A behavioral explanation would look at reinforcement and learning, not at how she interprets the grade.

why.correct: The psychodynamic perspective explains disorders through unconscious conflicts, often from childhood, kept out of awareness by defense mechanisms.
options: The humanistic perspective focuses on growth and self-concept in the present, not on unconscious conflicts.
Right: unconscious conflicts from early relationships, held back by defense mechanisms, are the psychodynamic explanation.
The cognitive perspective looks at conscious thought patterns, not at conflicts kept out of awareness.
The biological perspective looks at the brain, genes and body chemistry, not at early relationships.

why.correct: The evolutionary perspective says people are prepared to fear dangers that threatened survival for our ancestors, so those fears are common.
options: Right: fears of dangers our ancestors faced, such as snakes and heights, may have helped them survive and are learned more easily.
The humanistic perspective is about self-concept and growth, and it says nothing about which fears are common.
The psychodynamic perspective looks at a person's unconscious conflicts, not at why some fears are common across people.
A cognitive account would focus on a person's thoughts, but it does not explain why ancient dangers are feared more than modern ones.

why.correct: The humanistic perspective links distress to conditional regard and to a mismatch between the self a person thinks they should be and their real experience.
options: A behavioral account would look at what reinforced his behavior, not at a gap between his self-concept and experience.
A biological account would look at genes or brain chemistry, not at conditional love and self-concept.
A sociocultural account would look at wider cultural or economic conditions, not at his self-concept.
Right: love that depends on conditions and a gap between self-concept and experience are the humanistic explanation.

why.correct: The biopsychosocial model explains a disorder as the product of biological, psychological and social factors acting together.
options: Self-blame is cognitive, but the clinician also weighs family history and social conditions.
The ICD is a classification system. It does not combine causes into an explanation.
Right: family history (biological), self-blame (psychological) and job loss in a hard economy (social) are combined.
Nothing here is about survival value. The clinician combines biological, psychological and social factors.

why.correct: The eclectic approach uses ideas and methods from several perspectives instead of one, matched to the person.
options: The diathesis-stress model explains why a disorder appears. It is not about choosing methods from several perspectives.
Right: drawing on several perspectives and choosing what fits each client is the eclectic approach.
Facing feared situations is behavioral, but she also uses cognitive and psychodynamic methods.
The DSM-5-TR classifies disorders. It does not tell a therapist which perspective to use.

why.correct: In the diathesis-stress model a vulnerability alone is not enough: a disorder appears when vulnerability meets enough stress.
options: Right: both share the vulnerability (diathesis), but only Ana met a major stressor, so only she developed depression.
The eclectic approach is about drawing on several perspectives in treatment, not about why one twin became ill.
The evolutionary perspective explains why traits are common, not why one twin and not the other developed depression.
Nothing in the scenario points to unconscious conflicts. The difference is the stressful event.

why.correct: The sociocultural perspective explains disorders through culture, social roles and conditions such as poverty and discrimination.
options: The humanistic perspective is about self-concept and growth, not about poverty and discrimination.
The biological perspective looks at genes and the brain, not at social conditions.
The psychodynamic perspective looks at unconscious conflicts, not at social conditions across groups.
Right: poverty, discrimination and economic conditions are social and cultural factors.

why.correct: With equal stress, the person with the greater diathesis is the one whose total passes the threshold.
options: The stress bars for Person 1 and Person 2 are the same height. The difference is vulnerability.
Person 1's vulnerability bar is the tallest in the figure.
Right: the stress is the same size, so the larger vulnerability carries Person 1 over the threshold.
Person 2's bar ends well below the dashed threshold line.

why.correct: In the model, total load is vulnerability plus stress. Person 2 and Person 3 have the same vulnerability, so equal stress gives the same result.
options: Person 3 has the same vulnerability and passes the threshold with that stress, so Person 2 would as well.
Right: Person 2 has the same small vulnerability as Person 3, so the same large stress would carry Person 2 over the threshold too.
Stress does not remove a vulnerability. The two add together in the model.
The threshold is the same line for everyone in the model.

why.correct: Person 3 has a small vulnerability and a very large stress, and the stress alone carries the total over the threshold.
options: Right: low vulnerability but a very large stress, like Person 3.
That is high vulnerability with small stress, the pattern of Person 1.
That is high vulnerability with little stress, which matches none of the bars.
That is low vulnerability with small stress, the pattern of Person 2.

why.correct: The 32% cell, family history plus 3 or more events, is the highest.
options: That group reached 14%, less than half of the 32% for the family-history group.
That group had 10%, one of the lowest values.
That group had 18%, lower than the 32% at 3 or more events.
Right: 32% is the highest value in the table.

why.correct: In the "Yes" row, <math class="psy-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>32</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>22</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">32 - 10 = 22</annotation></semantics></math> percentage points.
The diathesis-stress model predicts the largest effect where vulnerability and stress meet, and the 32% cell shows that.
options: They did have some, 6% to 14%. The model does not say a vulnerability is required.
Right: with a family history the rate climbed from 10% to 32%; without one it climbed from 6% to 14%. Vulnerability and stress combine.
The rate rose with more events in both rows.
The gap between rows grew from 4 points at 0 events to 18 points at 3 or more events.

why.correct: Because nothing was manipulated, this is correlational research. It shows a relationship; a third variable, such as financial hardship, could produce both.
options: Right: this is a correlational study, so a third variable, such as poverty, could explain the links.
A causal claim needs an experiment with random assignment. Nothing was manipulated here.
The rates were higher in the "Yes" row at every level of stress.
Generalizing depends on who was studied, and the table tells us only about these 600 adults.

why.correct: The label was manipulated and students were randomly assigned, so the study is an experiment.
options: A correlational study measures variables without manipulating them. Here the label was manipulated.
A case study looks at one person in depth. This study compared 120 students in two conditions.
Students were not watched in a natural setting. They read a description and gave a rating.
Right: the researchers manipulated the label and randomly assigned students to versions.

why.correct: An operational definition says exactly how the study measured the variable: the question asked and the scale used.
Statistically significant means a difference this large would rarely happen by chance alone, so the label probably made a real difference for these students.
options: A mean is an average. Individual students gave different ratings.
Right: statistical significance means the difference is unlikely to have happened by chance.
Significance is not size. A small difference can be significant in a large sample.
Significance says nothing about who the results generalize to.

why.correct: Informed consent is in the summary: students read a consent form and agreed in writing. Review by the institutional review board is also described.
options: Right: the summary says each student read a consent form and agreed in writing.
Random assignment is a design feature, not an ethical safeguard.
The summary does not mention payment.
The summary describes no follow-up interview.

why.correct: A long-lasting low mood (two years or more in adults), often milder than a major depressive episode, fits persistent depressive disorder.
options: Bipolar II needs at least one hypomanic episode, a period of unusually high energy and mood. Marcus has none.
Generalized anxiety disorder centers on excessive worry, not on a long-lasting low mood.
PTSD follows a traumatic event and centers on intrusive memories, avoidance and feeling on edge. No trauma is described.
Right: a depressed mood on most days for at least two years in an adult is the core of persistent depressive disorder.

why.correct: Bipolar I disorder is defined by at least one manic episode. Many people with bipolar I also have depressive episodes, but one is not needed for the diagnosis.
options: Bipolar II involves hypomania, a milder high that does not seriously disrupt life, plus a major depressive episode. Jordan's episode is severe and he has had no depression.
Major depressive disorder involves low mood or loss of interest, the opposite of Jordan's high energy.
Right: a full manic episode lasting at least a week, with reduced need for sleep, racing speech, risky spending and grandiosity, defines bipolar I. A depressive episode is not required.
Generalized anxiety disorder is about ongoing worry, not about a long stretch of high energy and grandiosity.

why.correct: Bipolar II combines at least one hypomanic episode with at least one major depressive episode, and never a full manic one.
options: Bipolar I needs a full manic episode, severe enough to seriously disrupt life. Kim's high was milder and she kept working.
Right: a hypomanic episode (a milder high of at least four days) plus a major depressive episode is the pattern of bipolar II.
Persistent depressive disorder is a long low mood with no periods of high energy.
Major depressive disorder fits the depression, but it does not explain the period of high energy.

why.correct: A hallucination is a false perception, most often hearing voices in schizophrenia. It is a positive symptom because it adds an experience.
options: Right: perceiving something, here a voice, that is not there is a hallucination.
A delusion is a false belief held despite clear evidence. Hearing a voice is a false perception.
Negative symptoms are losses, such as flat emotion or little speech. Hearing a voice adds something.
A compulsion is a repeated act done to reduce anxiety, as in obsessive-compulsive disorder.

why.correct: Delusions are false beliefs held firmly in spite of evidence; beliefs about being watched or controlled are common in schizophrenia.
options: A hallucination is a false perception, such as hearing or seeing something. Elena holds a false belief.
An obsession is an unwanted thought the person usually knows is excessive and tries to push away. Elena is convinced hers is true.
Flat affect is a lack of emotional expression, a negative symptom, not a false belief.
Right: a fixed false belief that does not change with clear evidence is a delusion.

why.correct: Negative symptoms are the absence or reduction of normal behavior; "positive" and "negative" mean added and taken away, not good and bad.
options: Positive symptoms add experiences, such as hallucinations and delusions. Dev shows losses instead.
Mania involves high energy and fast speech, the opposite of what Dev shows.
Right: withdrawal, little speech, flat expression and low motivation are losses of normal functions, which are negative symptoms.
Dissociative symptoms involve gaps in memory or identity, not withdrawal and flat expression.

why.correct: "Split personality" confuses schizophrenia with dissociative identity disorder. In schizophrenia the "split" is from reality: false perceptions and beliefs.
options: Schizophrenia is in the schizophrenia spectrum, not among the mood disorders.
Right: schizophrenia involves symptoms such as hallucinations and delusions. Distinct identity states belong to dissociative identity disorder.
Schizophrenia does not involve separate identities at all.
Schizophrenia usually begins in late adolescence or early adulthood, not in early childhood.

why.correct: Dissociative identity disorder involves two or more distinct identity states and recurrent gaps in memory. Some researchers debate how often it arises from trauma versus from social and therapeutic influences.
options: Right: two or more distinct identity states with gaps in memory are the core of dissociative identity disorder.
Schizophrenia involves hallucinations, delusions or negative symptoms, not distinct identity states.
Bipolar I involves shifts in mood and energy, not separate identities with memory gaps.
Borderline personality disorder involves unstable emotions and relationships, not distinct identity states.

why.correct: Dissociative amnesia is memory loss, usually for personal and stressful information, that is not ordinary forgetting or the result of injury. "With fugue" adds wandering or travel.
options: Anterograde amnesia is trouble forming new memories after brain injury. Doctors found no injury, and he lost old memories.
He has lost his identity, not shifted between two or more distinct identity states.
PTSD involves vivid, unwanted memories of the trauma, not loss of memory for one's whole identity.
Right: loss of memory for one's identity and past, with travel away from home, after a stressful event and no physical cause, is dissociative amnesia with fugue.

why.correct: Panic disorder means unexpected panic attacks plus ongoing worry about future attacks or changes in behavior to avoid them.
options: A specific phobia is fear of one object or situation. Sasha's attacks come out of the blue.
Social anxiety centers on fear of being judged by others. Her attacks happen even when she is alone.
Right: repeated unexpected panic attacks followed by at least a month of worry about more attacks define panic disorder.
Bipolar II involves periods of high and low mood, not sudden attacks of intense fear.

why.correct: Agoraphobia is fear of situations such as crowds, public transportation or lines because escape might be difficult or help unavailable.
options: A specific phobia focuses on one object or situation, such as spiders. Omar fears many places for the same reason.
Right: fear and avoidance of several situations where escape or help might be hard to reach is agoraphobia.
Generalized anxiety disorder is broad worry about many life matters, not fear of places where escape is hard.
His avoidance is not a repeated ritual done to quiet an intrusive thought.

why.correct: Social anxiety disorder centers on fear of scrutiny and negative evaluation, which leads people to avoid or dread social situations.
options: Right: intense fear of being judged or embarrassed in social situations, with avoidance, is social anxiety disorder.
Agoraphobia is fear of places where escape is hard. Leah's fear is of being judged.
Panic disorder involves unexpected attacks. Leah's fear is predictable and tied to being watched.
Avoidant personality disorder is a long-lasting pattern across most relationships, not a fear focused on performance situations.

why.correct: Generalized anxiety disorder is excessive, hard-to-control worry about many topics for at least six months, with symptoms such as tension, fatigue and poor sleep.
options: Panic disorder centers on sudden attacks of intense fear. Paolo has steady worry, not attacks.
A specific phobia is fear of one object or situation. Paolo worries about many things.
Persistent depressive disorder is a long low mood. Paolo's main problem is worry.
Right: hard-to-control worry about many things, on most days for six months or more, with tension and poor sleep, is generalized anxiety disorder.

why.correct: In obsessive-compulsive disorder, obsessions raise anxiety and compulsions lower it for a while, which keeps the cycle going. The DSM-5-TR places it in its own category, apart from the anxiety disorders.
options: Generalized anxiety disorder involves broad worry without a ritual that the person feels driven to repeat.
That personality disorder is about perfectionism and control. It does not involve unwanted thoughts relieved by rituals.
Right: an intrusive thought (the obsession) and the repeated checking to relieve the anxiety (the compulsion) define obsessive-compulsive disorder.
Hoarding disorder is difficulty discarding possessions, not checking the stove.

why.correct: Hoarding disorder is in the obsessive-compulsive and related category; its core is difficulty parting with possessions, whatever their value.
options: Hoarding disorder is related to it, in the same DSM-5-TR category, but Glen's problem is saving and not discarding, not intrusive thoughts and rituals.
Right: persistent difficulty discarding possessions, distress at the thought of parting with them, and clutter that blocks living spaces describe hoarding disorder.
Depression can make cleaning hard, but it does not explain his distress at discarding objects.
Dependent personality disorder is about relying on others, not about saving possessions.

why.correct: PTSD follows exposure to a traumatic event and includes intrusive memories, avoidance, negative changes in thought and mood, and heightened arousal for over a month.
options: Right: after a traumatic event, intrusive memories, avoidance, negative mood and high arousal lasting more than a month define PTSD.
A phobia of driving would not explain the flashbacks, nightmares and constant jumpiness that followed a trauma.
Panic disorder involves unexpected attacks. Ana's symptoms are tied to the memory of the crash.
Dissociative amnesia involves losing memories. Ana has too much memory of the event, not too little.

why.correct: Bulimia nervosa involves cycles of binge eating and compensating behaviors; people with it are often at an average weight, which is one way to tell it from anorexia nervosa.
options: Anorexia nervosa involves a significantly low body weight from restricting food. Her weight is in the normal range.
Her eating pattern is not a ritual done to quiet an intrusive thought.
Changes in appetite can occur in depression, but binges followed by fasting point to an eating disorder.
Right: repeated binge eating followed by behaviors to make up for it, often at a normal weight, is bulimia nervosa.

why.correct: ADHD is a neurodevelopmental disorder: inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity that begins in childhood and appears in more than one setting, such as home and school.
options: Autism spectrum disorder centers on differences in social communication plus restricted, repetitive behaviors or interests.
Worry can disturb focus, but nothing here describes excessive worry.
Right: a lasting pattern of inattention and hyperactivity or impulsivity that began in childhood and shows up in two or more settings fits ADHD.
Bipolar I involves distinct episodes of mania, not a steady pattern since early childhood.

why.correct: Autism spectrum disorder is a neurodevelopmental disorder with two core features, and "spectrum" means support needs range widely.
options: Lining up toys is repetitive, but OCD does not explain the differences in social communication from early childhood.
Right: differences in social communication plus restricted, repetitive behaviors from early childhood are the two core features of autism spectrum disorder.
ADHD is about inattention and hyperactivity, not social communication with insistence on sameness.
Social anxiety is fear of being judged. Nothing here suggests fear of judgment.

why.correct: Cluster A, odd or eccentric, includes paranoid, schizoid and schizotypal personality disorders. Paranoid personality disorder is pervasive distrust of others.
options: Right: lasting, widespread distrust and suspicion is paranoid personality disorder, in Cluster A.
Cluster B includes antisocial, histrionic, narcissistic and borderline personality disorders, none of which centers on distrust.
Cluster C includes avoidant, dependent and obsessive-compulsive personality disorders, which center on anxiety, not suspicion.
His suspicion is a lasting personality pattern, not a fixed false belief from a psychotic disorder such as schizophrenia.

why.correct: Antisocial personality disorder, in Cluster B, is diagnosed in adults with a pattern of disregard for others' rights that began in childhood or the early teen years.
options: Avoidant personality disorder involves shyness and fear of rejection, the opposite of disregard for others.
Schizoid personality disorder is detachment from relationships, not harming and deceiving others.
Dependent personality disorder is an excessive need to be cared for by others.
Right: a lasting disregard for and violation of other people's rights, with little remorse, is antisocial personality disorder, in Cluster B.

why.correct: The names are similar, but OCD involves unwanted thoughts and rituals that relieve anxiety, while obsessive-compulsive personality disorder is a lasting, perfectionistic way of relating to tasks and people.
options: OCD involves unwanted intrusive thoughts and rituals to relieve them. Mei has no intrusive thoughts and sees her habits as right.
Generalized anxiety disorder is worry about many things, not a lasting need for order and control.
Right: a lasting focus on order, perfection and control, without true obsessions or compulsions, is obsessive-compulsive personality disorder, in Cluster C.
Narcissistic personality disorder centers on a need for admiration, not on rules and perfection.

why.correct: Culture-bound syndromes (the DSM-5-TR calls them cultural concepts of distress) show how culture shapes symptoms. Taijin kyofusho focuses on the fear of offending others, unlike social anxiety, which focuses on fear of embarrassing oneself.
options: Agoraphobia is fear of places where escape is hard, not fear of offending others.
Right: taijin kyofusho, a fear of offending others with one's body or behavior, is an example of how culture shapes the form distress takes.
That disorder involves distrust of others, not fear that one's own body offends them.
Ataque de nervios is a different cultural example: an episode of intense distress, such as shouting, crying and trembling, after a stressful event.

why.correct: The dopamine hypothesis is a biological explanation of the positive symptoms of schizophrenia. It is part of the picture, not a complete explanation.
options: Right: the hypothesis links too much dopamine activity to positive symptoms such as hallucinations and delusions.
That model is about vulnerability plus stress. These findings are about one neurotransmitter and psychotic symptoms.
These findings are about brain chemistry, not about patterns of thinking.
Phobias are not involved, and the findings are biological, not about learning.

why.correct: Positive symptoms add something (hallucinations, delusions, disorganized speech); negative symptoms take something away (emotion, speech, motivation).
options: Right: a hallucination adds an experience, so it is a positive symptom.
Flat affect is the loss of normal expression, a negative symptom.
Right: this is a delusion, a false belief added to experience, so it is a positive symptom.
Reduced speech is a loss of normal behavior, a negative symptom.
Withdrawal and low motivation are losses of normal functions, negative symptoms.

why.correct: Since the DSM-5 (2013), and still in the DSM-5-TR, PTSD has been in the trauma- and stressor-related category rather than with the anxiety disorders, as the figure shows.
options: Anxiety is a large part of PTSD, but the figure and the DSM-5-TR place it in the trauma- and stressor-related category.
Dissociative disorders involve gaps in memory or identity. PTSD has its own category.
Right: the figure places PTSD in its own category, defined by exposure to a traumatic event.
Depressive disorders center on low mood and loss of interest. PTSD follows trauma.

why.correct: The figure groups obsessive-compulsive disorder with hoarding disorder, apart from the anxiety disorders.
options: They are in different boxes: generalized anxiety is with the anxiety disorders.
Right: both are in the obsessive-compulsive and related category.
The figure gives depressive and bipolar disorders separate boxes.
They are in different categories, and confusing them is a common error.

why.correct: The bipolar disorders are set apart by manic or hypomanic episodes. Low mood can occur in both categories.
options: Right: what defines the bipolar disorders is a period of abnormally high mood and energy, which depressive disorders never include.
Many people with bipolar disorder also have depressive episodes; bipolar II requires one.
They are mood-related disorders with episodes, not lasting personality patterns.
Depressive disorders can begin at any age.

why.correct: Personality disorders are enduring, inflexible patterns of thinking, feeling and relating that differ from cultural expectations and cause distress or dysfunction.
options: Anxiety disorders center on fear and worry, not on a lifelong, rigid way of relating to everyone.
Nothing here mentions hallucinations, delusions or negative symptoms.
Neurodevelopmental disorders begin in early childhood and include ADHD and autism spectrum disorder.
Right: a lasting, inflexible pattern that begins by adolescence or early adulthood and shows up across settings is a personality disorder.

why.correct: Shared diagnosis rises with genetic relatedness, which points to a genetic contribution.
options: Identical twins are at 46%, about three times the 15% for fraternal twins.
Siblings are at 9%, far below the 46% for identical twins.
Right: identical twins (all genes shared) are highest, then fraternal twins and siblings, then unrelated people.
Each kind of relative is well above the 1% for unrelated people.

why.correct: <math class="psy-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>46</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>15</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>31</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">46 - 15 = 31</annotation></semantics></math> percentage points.
A genetic vulnerability raises risk but does not decide the outcome; this is the diathesis-stress idea applied to schizophrenia.
options: Right: if genes were the whole story, identical twins would match far more often. A vulnerability plus environmental stress fits the diathesis-stress model.
The steady rise with genetic relatedness shows genes do play a part.
Nothing in the graph suggests an error. A match well under 100% is expected when environment also matters.
Being a twin is not a cause; the unrelated group gives the base rate for comparison.

why.correct: Genes and a shared home are confounded in twins raised together, so the correlation alone cannot prove that genes are the cause.
options: Twins are often studied. The issue is that genes and environment are tangled together.
Twins raised together share much of their environment, which is the problem.
Identical twins share all their genes; fraternal twins share about half, like other siblings.
Right: twins share a home as well as genes, so a shared environment could explain part of the match. Adoption studies help separate the two.

why.correct: Exposure was measured, not manipulated, so the study is correlational.
options: An experiment needs a manipulated variable and random assignment. No one was assigned to a hurricane danger.
A case study looks at one person in depth. This study measured seven adults on the same two variables.
Right: the researchers measured exposure and symptoms as they occurred and looked at their relationship, without assigning exposure.
Researchers did not watch behavior in a natural setting. Adults reported their own exposure and symptoms.

why.correct: In order the scores are 8, 12, 15, 22, 30, 41, 48. With seven scores, the median is the fourth: 22.
The study shows a strong positive relationship, but a third variable, such as poverty or lack of support, could produce both.
options: Right: for example, adults with fewer resources may have faced more danger and also had less support afterward.
No correlation, however strong, proves cause on its own. Exposure was not manipulated.
Timing helps, but without manipulation a third variable could still explain the link.
The correlation is positive, 0.78: more exposure went with more symptoms.

why.correct: Generalize from who was studied: adults from one coastal town after a hurricane. A small, volunteer sample limits the claim further.
options: No children took part, and only one kind of disaster was studied.
The sample was seven volunteers from one town, after one hurricane.
Combat is a different kind of trauma from a hurricane, and no soldiers were studied.
Right: the volunteers were adults from one coastal town after a hurricane, so the results best fit similar adults in similar settings.

why.correct: Name a safeguard the summary actually describes. Here: informed consent, and confidentiality through numbers in place of names.
options: The summary describes no deception and no debriefing.
No one was assigned to a level of danger, and random assignment is a design feature, not an ethical safeguard.
Right: the summary says the researchers kept names confidential by giving each person a number.
The right to withdraw is a real safeguard, but this summary does not describe it.

why.correct: Person B's line shows a high stretch and a later low stretch; Person A's shows only a low stretch.
options: Person A dips to 2 and returns to 5, but never rises far above 5.
Right: Person B rises to 9 in weeks 4 to 6 and falls to 2 in weeks 9 to 11.
Only Person B has a high period. Person A only dips.
Person B clearly shows both a high and a low period.

why.correct: Once a full manic episode has occurred, the diagnosis is bipolar I, whether or not there is also depression.
options: Right: a full manic episode is what defines bipolar I; the depressive episode is common but not required.
Major depressive disorder has no manic episodes. The high period rules it out.
That is a long, steady low mood, not a high followed by a low.
Bipolar II involves hypomania, a milder high, and never a full manic episode.

why.correct: <math class="psy-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mn>4</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>3.25</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{5 + 4 + 2 + 2}{4} = 3.25</annotation></semantics></math>.
A major depressive episode needs five or more symptoms, including low mood or loss of interest, for at least two weeks.
options: Two years is the rule for persistent depressive disorder in adults, not for a major depressive episode.
Six months is the rule for generalized anxiety disorder, not for a depressive episode.
Right: a major depressive episode requires symptoms on most days for at least two weeks.
One day is far too short. A major depressive episode needs two weeks.

why.correct: Free association comes from psychodynamic therapy: unguarded talk may reveal unconscious conflicts.
options: Active listening is the person-centered therapist echoing and clarifying feelings, not looking for hidden conflicts.
Cognitive restructuring targets conscious, distorted thoughts and replaces them with more accurate ones.
Systematic desensitization pairs relaxation with feared situations. It is a behavioral technique.
Right: saying whatever comes to mind, so the therapist can look for unconscious themes, is free association, a psychodynamic technique.

why.correct: Person-centered therapy offers genuineness, empathy shown through active listening, and unconditional positive regard, and the client directs the work.
options: A cognitive therapist would actively challenge distorted thoughts, not mainly reflect feelings.
A psychodynamic therapist would interpret unconscious conflicts, not mainly mirror feelings.
Right: active listening, unconditional positive regard and a client-led session are the core of person-centered (humanistic) therapy.
Aversion therapy pairs an unwanted behavior with an unpleasant stimulus. It is behavioral.

why.correct: Systematic desensitization counterconditions a fear: relaxation, which is incompatible with anxiety, is paired with feared scenes step by step.
options: Aversion therapy pairs an unwanted behavior with something unpleasant, the reverse of pairing fear with relaxation.
Right: relaxation paired with a step-by-step hierarchy of feared scenes is systematic desensitization, a form of counterconditioning.
A token economy rewards target behaviors with tokens. Nothing is being rewarded here.
Free association is a psychodynamic technique of saying whatever comes to mind.

why.correct: Aversion therapy uses classical conditioning to attach an unpleasant response to an unwanted behavior. Its effects often fade unless other supports are added.
options: Right: alcohol (the conditioned stimulus) is paired with nausea, so alcohol alone comes to trigger queasiness.
A token economy rewards a target behavior with tokens. Here something unpleasant is paired with alcohol.
Exposure reduces a fear by facing it without harm. This method creates an unpleasant response.
Biofeedback shows a person their own body signals, such as heart rate, so they can learn to control them.

why.correct: A token economy uses secondary reinforcers, the tokens, to strengthen desired behaviors through operant conditioning.
options: Aversion therapy pairs an unwanted behavior with something unpleasant. Here desired behaviors are rewarded.
Systematic desensitization reduces fear with relaxation. Nothing here is about fear.
Group therapy is talk in a group led by a therapist, not trading tokens for rewards.
Right: tokens (secondary reinforcers) given for target behaviors and traded for rewards are a token economy, an operant technique.

why.correct: Biofeedback gives information about body processes such as muscle tension or heart rate so a person can learn to control them.
options: TMS uses magnetic pulses on the scalp to stimulate the brain. Nothing is applied to her brain here.
Exposure therapy is facing a feared stimulus. She is learning to control a body signal.
Right: showing a person a live signal from their own body so they can learn to change it is biofeedback.
Cognitive restructuring changes thoughts. Here she learns to change a body response using feedback.

why.correct: REBT, a cognitive therapy, confronts irrational beliefs such as "I must be liked by everyone" and replaces them with more realistic ones.
options: A person-centered therapist would not argue with the client's beliefs but would reflect feelings without judgment.
Right: directly and forcefully disputing irrational "must" beliefs is the hallmark of REBT.
A psychodynamic therapist would look for unconscious roots, not dispute the belief head on.
That behavioral technique pairs relaxation with feared scenes; it does not dispute beliefs.

why.correct: The cognitive triad is negative thinking about oneself, the world and the future. Cognitive therapy helps people test and change these thoughts.
options: Right: negative views of the self, the world and the future are the cognitive triad that cognitive therapy targets in depression.
Learned helplessness is giving up after uncontrollable events. The scenario describes three kinds of negative thoughts.
That is the accepting attitude of a person-centered therapist, not a pattern of client thoughts.
Free association is a psychodynamic technique, not a set of negative beliefs.

why.correct: DBT was developed for people with intense emotions and self-harm, including many with borderline personality disorder; it combines acceptance with skills for change.
options: REBT disputes irrational beliefs. It does not center on mindfulness and distress-tolerance skills.
Aversion therapy pairs a behavior with something unpleasant. It does not teach coping skills.
Psychodynamic therapy explores unconscious conflicts rather than teaching specific skills.
Right: DBT, a form of CBT, blends acceptance with change and teaches mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation and relationship skills.

why.correct: Group and family formats let people see they are not alone, practice new ways of relating and change patterns in a whole system; they also cost less per person.
options: No one format is best for every disorder. The choice depends on the problem and the people.
An alliance still matters, now with each family member.
Right: family and group therapy treat the person within a system of relationships, so patterns between people can change.
Most psychologists do not prescribe, and the format has nothing to do with medication.

why.correct: Across many kinds of therapy, a strong therapeutic alliance predicts better outcomes.
options: Deinstitutionalization is the move of patients out of hospitals into community care, not a feature of a therapy relationship.
Right: the bond of trust between therapist and client, with agreement on goals and tasks, is one of the strongest predictors of improvement.
The placebo effect is improvement from expectations alone. Both groups expected treatment; the difference was the relationship.
Aversion therapy is a behavioral technique, and both therapists used the same method.

why.correct: Cultural humility means staying curious about each client's culture and being honest about one's own limits, which supports the therapeutic alliance.
options: Right: an ongoing attitude of learning from clients about their culture, and recognizing the limits of one's own view, is cultural humility.
The eclectic approach is about mixing methods from several perspectives, not about learning a client's cultural view.
Ethnocentrism is judging other cultures by one's own, the opposite of what she does.
Free association is a psychodynamic technique, not an attitude toward a client's culture.

why.correct: Deinstitutionalization moved care from large hospitals to communities; without enough community services, many people were left without care.
options: Psychosurgery is brain surgery to change behavior, not the move out of hospitals.
Cultural humility is an attitude in therapy, not a change in where patients live.
The alliance is the bond in therapy, not a shift in hospital policy.
Right: moving patients out of hospitals is deinstitutionalization, and underfunded community care left many people without support, some homeless.

why.correct: Lithium stabilizes mood in bipolar disorder and lowers suicide risk; its narrow safe range requires regular blood tests.
options: An SSRI treats depression and anxiety. Given alone in bipolar disorder, it can risk triggering mania.
Anti-anxiety drugs calm anxiety; they do not prevent manic episodes.
Right: lithium is a mood stabilizer for bipolar disorder that needs blood tests because its safe range is narrow.
Some antipsychotics are used in bipolar disorder, but the blood-level monitoring described here points to lithium.

why.correct: Antipsychotics act as dopamine antagonists. Tardive dyskinesia, involuntary facial and tongue movements, can follow long-term use and may not go away.
options: Antidepressants target serotonin and other transmitters, not dopamine receptors, and do not mainly treat hallucinations.
Right: antipsychotics block dopamine receptors to reduce positive symptoms; long-term use, especially of older ones, can cause tardive dyskinesia.
Lithium is a mood stabilizer for bipolar disorder. It does not block dopamine receptors.
Anti-anxiety drugs act on GABA, not on dopamine receptors, and do not reduce hallucinations.

why.correct: ECT is an effective treatment for severe, treatment-resistant depression; short-term memory loss around the treatment period is its main side effect.
options: Right: a brief, controlled seizure under anesthesia, used mainly for severe depression that has not responded to other treatments, is ECT.
TMS uses magnetic pulses through the scalp while the person is awake, with no seizure and no anesthesia.
Psychosurgery removes or destroys brain tissue. ECT removes no tissue.
Biofeedback teaches a person to control body signals. It does not involve electric current or seizures.

why.correct: TMS stimulates targeted brain areas with magnetic pulses and is used for depression that has not responded to medication; it needs no anesthesia.
options: ECT uses electric current to cause a seizure under anesthesia. She is awake and has no seizure.
A lobotomy cut connections to the frontal lobes. It is surgery, now abandoned.
Biofeedback shows a person their body signals. TMS applies magnetic pulses to the brain.
Right: magnetic pulses through the scalp to the brain, with the person awake, is TMS.

why.correct: Hypnosis can help with pain and anxiety, but it does not recover accurate memories or regress people to an earlier age.
options: Research does not support this. Hypnosis raises confidence but also false memories.
Age regression under hypnosis does not take people back. They act out what they expect.
Right: under hypnosis, people report more "memories" and feel more sure of them, but false memories increase too.
Hypnosis has some evidence for reducing pain and anxiety when combined with other treatment.

why.correct: Evidence-based practice joins the best research evidence with clinical expertise and the client's culture, values and preferences.
options: The eclectic approach draws on several perspectives, but it does not by itself require weighing research evidence.
Right: combining the best research, clinical expertise and the client's characteristics and preferences is evidence-based practice.
Deinstitutionalization was a shift from hospitals to community care.
Cultural humility is one part of good care, but the approach described also weighs research and expertise.

why.correct: Therapists protect confidentiality. Exceptions are narrow, such as a serious risk of harm to the client or others, and clients are told about them at the start.
options: Right: without the client's written permission, therapists keep what clients say private. The main exceptions involve serious risk of harm.
Concern is not permission. Sharing would break confidentiality.
A job being at stake does not override confidentiality without the client's consent.
A diagnosis is private health information too; sharing it breaks confidentiality.

why.correct: Anti-anxiety drugs that act on GABA work quickly but carry risks of tolerance, dependence and withdrawal, so they are often limited to short-term use.
options: Drugs of this kind act within minutes to hours, which is part of why they are used for short periods.
Blocking dopamine is what antipsychotics do. This drug increases GABA's effect.
That describes lithium, used for bipolar disorder.
Right: drugs that boost GABA, such as benzodiazepines, calm anxiety fast, but regular use can lead to tolerance, dependence and withdrawal.

why.correct: Exposure starts with a ranked list, then works up one step at a time, staying with each step until the fear falls, so the fear extinguishes without the feared harm.
The independent variable is what the researchers manipulated: the treatment condition.
options: That is the dependent variable, what was measured.
Right: the researchers manipulated which condition each participant received.
Age was not manipulated; it describes the sample.
The interviewer was kept unaware to reduce bias. That is a design feature, not the independent variable.

why.correct: The waitlist is the control group: it shows how symptoms change over 12 weeks with no study treatment, which may include natural improvement and the effect of expecting help later.
options: Right: depression often eases somewhat on its own; the waitlist group is a control showing that change, so the treatment effects can be judged against it.
The waitlist group received no study treatment during the 12 weeks.
All groups started at 30, but the waitlist is there as a comparison, not to equalize scores.
The question was whether treatments beat waiting, not whether waiting harms. Scores in that group actually fell a little.

why.correct: Not statistically significant means the difference could plausibly be due to chance; it does not prove the two treatments are identical.
options: Both groups improved significantly more than the waitlist. The non-significant result is only about CBT compared with medication.
The CBT mean (16) was slightly lower, and the difference was not significant either way.
Statistical significance has nothing to do with ethics.
Right: "not statistically significant" means the gap of 1 point could be due to chance, so neither treatment can be called better from this study.

why.correct: The summary describes informed consent, the right to withdraw and institutional review board approval. Offering waitlisted people treatment afterward also protects them.
options: No deception is described, so no debriefing after deception is mentioned.
Random assignment is a design feature that supports causal claims, not an ethical safeguard.
Right: the summary says participants were told they could leave the study at any time.
Keeping the interviewer unaware reduces bias. It is a design feature, not an ethical safeguard.

why.correct: Generalize to people like the participants: adults with diagnosed major depressive disorder in similar community clinics.
options: No teenagers took part, and all participants had major depressive disorder.
Right: the participants were adults 18 to 65 diagnosed with major depressive disorder at community clinics in one US state.
No participants had schizophrenia, and they were recruited at community clinics.
Feeling sad at times is not a diagnosis, and the sample came from one US state.

why.correct: <math class="psy-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>28</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>12</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">28 - 12 = 16</annotation></semantics></math> points.

<math class="psy-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>16</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><mn>3</mn></mfrac><mo>≈</mo><mn>9.67</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{16 + 10 + 3}{3} \approx 9.67</annotation></semantics></math> points.
Compare the drops: 16 for exposure, 10 for medication, 3 for the waitlist.
options: Medication fell 10 points, less than exposure therapy's 16.
The waitlist fell 3 points, far less than medication's 10.
Right: exposure fell 16 points, medication 10 and the waitlist 3.
Every group's score fell, by 3 to 16 points.

why.correct: Control groups show the change that happens without the treatment, from time, natural recovery and expectations, so the treatment effect is the extra change beyond it.
options: Nothing in the summary suggests this. Some change without treatment is common.
Right: natural improvement over time and expectations can lower scores, which is why a control group is needed for comparison.
Scores can rise or fall. The waitlist simply improved a little.
All 60 adults had social anxiety disorder.

why.correct: Random assignment makes groups equivalent on average, so differences after treatment can be attributed to the independent variable.
options: Right: random assignment spreads differences between people evenly across groups, so a later difference can be traced to the treatment.
That is random sampling, which affects generalizing, not random assignment.
Random assignment does not remove measurement error.
Random assignment says nothing about the population mean.

why.correct: A conscious, distorted belief is the target of cognitive approaches such as cognitive restructuring.
options: Biomedical treatments target brain chemistry and activity, not a specific belief.
Psychodynamic therapy targets unconscious conflicts, not conscious distorted beliefs.
Humanistic therapy supports growth and self-acceptance but does not directly challenge the belief.
Right: the figure says the cognitive approach targets distorted, negative thoughts, such as this belief.

why.correct: Behavioral techniques apply classical and operant conditioning: exposure, systematic desensitization, aversion therapy and token economies.
options: Those are psychodynamic techniques.
Those belong to humanistic, person-centered therapy.
Right: both are listed under behavioral, since both change learned behavior through conditioning.
Those are biomedical treatments.

why.correct: Psychodynamic therapy seeks insight into unconscious conflicts rooted in earlier experience.
options: Behavioral therapy changes current behavior through conditioning, not insight into early relationships.
Right: exploring how early experiences and unconscious conflicts shape the present is the psychodynamic goal.
CBT focuses on present thoughts and behaviors, not on unconscious roots in early relationships.
Biomedical treatments change brain chemistry or activity and do not aim at insight.

why.correct: The biomedical row targets brain chemistry and activity: medication, TMS, ECT and, rarely, psychosurgery.
options: Right: the biomedical row lists medication, TMS and ECT, which are used when psychotherapy alone has not helped.
Humanistic therapy is a psychotherapy, and she has already tried several.
Psychodynamic therapy is another psychotherapy, not a next step beyond them.
Behavioral techniques are psychotherapy too; the figure places medication and brain stimulation under biomedical.

why.correct: Cognitive therapy changes thoughts; CBT changes thoughts and behaviors together.
options: That is the psychodynamic row.
That is the biomedical row.
Reflecting feelings is active listening, in the humanistic row.
Right: both target thoughts; CBT adds direct work on behavior.
